data.sourceTitle: When a Hazard Becomes a Disaster
data.targetTitle: When a Hazard Becomes a Disaster
data.sourcePassage: A natural hazard is a natural event that could cause harm. It becomes a natural disaster when it seriously damages people, property, services, or the environment. Two earthquakes can have very different results. One may strike a remote desert where few people or buildings are exposed. Another may strike a crowded city with older buildings, busy roads, hospitals, schools, and water pipes underground. The second earthquake is more likely to become a disaster because exposure and vulnerability are higher. Geographers study both physical geography and human geography to understand this difference. They ask where the hazard happened, who lives there, how strong the infrastructure is, and how quickly people can get help.

questions.question: What is a natural hazard?
questions.modelAnswer: A natural event that could cause harm.

questions.question: Which situation is most likely to become a disaster?
questions.modelAnswer: A weaker earthquake in a crowded city with unsafe buildings.
options: A strong earthquake in an empty desert
A weaker earthquake in a crowded city with unsafe buildings
A storm that stays far out at sea
A volcano on an uninhabited island

questions.question: Why does exposure matter in disaster risk?
questions.modelAnswer: Exposure matters because people, buildings, and services in the hazard zone can be harmed.

questions.question: How does this passage connect physical and human geography?
questions.modelAnswer: It connects the natural event with human factors such as population, buildings, infrastructure, and emergency help.

data.sourcePassage: In March 2011, a very powerful earthquake occurred off the coast of Japan. It triggered a tsunami that caused major damage along the coast. Japan is located near active tectonic plate boundaries, so earthquake and tsunami hazards are part of its geography. Many communities also live along the coast, which increases exposure to tsunami waves. Warning systems, drills, maps, sea walls, and evacuation routes helped many people understand the danger, but the tsunami was still extremely destructive. This case study shows that preparedness can reduce risk but cannot remove all danger. Coastal land use, public education, and strong infrastructure all matter when communities face rare but severe hazards.

questions.question: What hazard triggered the tsunami in Japan in 2011?
questions.modelAnswer: A very powerful offshore earthquake triggered the tsunami.

questions.question: Why is Japan exposed to earthquake and tsunami hazards?
questions.modelAnswer: Japan is near active tectonic plate boundaries.
options: It is far from all plate boundaries
It is near active tectonic plate boundaries
It has no coastal settlements

questions.question: Why did preparedness not remove all danger in this case?
questions.modelAnswer: Preparedness helped many people, but the tsunami was still extremely powerful and affected exposed coastal communities.

questions.question: What lesson does this case study teach about resilience?
questions.modelAnswer: Resilience depends on warnings, education, evacuation routes, infrastructure, and learning from the event, but communities must still plan for severe impacts.

data.sourcePassage: Hurricane Katrina struck the Gulf Coast of the United States in 2005. New Orleans was especially affected when flood protection systems failed. The city is low-lying and near the Mississippi River delta, and some neighborhoods are below sea level. Wetlands that once helped absorb storm surge had been reduced. Human geography also shaped the disaster. Evacuation was harder for people without cars, money, or safe places to go. Katrina shows that disaster risk is not only about wind speed or rainfall. Infrastructure, social vulnerability, wetland loss, transport access, and coastal development all affect who is harmed and how quickly people can recover.

questions.modelAnswer: People without cars, money, or safe places to go found it harder to evacuate.

questions.question: Why are wetlands important in this case study?
questions.modelAnswer: Wetlands can absorb and slow storm surge, so wetland loss reduced natural protection.

data.sourcePassage: Drought is a long period with much less water than usual. It is often a slow-onset disaster because it develops over weeks, months, or even years. In the Horn of Africa, droughts have affected countries such as Somalia, Ethiopia, and Kenya. Some areas depend on seasonal rainfall, and many families rely on farming or herding animals. When rains fail, crops may die, livestock may weaken, food prices may rise, and water sources may shrink. People may migrate to search for water, pasture, jobs, safety, or aid. This shows how climate, resources, food, and population movement are connected. Sustainable water management and early warning systems can reduce harm.

questions.question: Why is drought both a physical and human geography issue?
questions.modelAnswer: It involves rainfall and climate, but also farming, water use, food prices, livelihoods, and migration.

data.sourcePassage: Riverbend Town is built beside a river because the land is flat, the soil is fertile, and the river provides water. Over time, the town has grown, and new homes are being built on the floodplain. Heavy rainstorms have become more intense in recent years. The town council is considering three choices: building a concrete flood wall, stopping new building on the highest-risk floodplain, and restoring wetlands upstream to absorb more water. A flood wall may reduce risk quickly in one area, but it can be expensive and may move water elsewhere. Stopping new building reduces future exposure. Wetland restoration can support long-term sustainability by storing water, filtering it, supporting wildlife, and reducing floods.

questions.question: Which option most directly reduces future exposure?
questions.modelAnswer: Stopping new building on the highest-risk floodplain reduces future exposure.
options: Build homes on more floodplain
Stop new building on the highest-risk floodplain
Remove all wetlands
Ignore heavier rainstorms

questions.question: What is one advantage of restoring wetlands upstream?
questions.modelAnswer: Wetlands can absorb and slow water while also supporting wildlife and water quality.

questions.question: Why might a town combine more than one flood solution?
questions.modelAnswer: Different solutions work at different speeds and scales, so combining them can protect existing areas while reducing long-term risk.
